attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: In context, 'the problem' means lawyers filing briefs with cases made up by LLMs. The normalisation keeps that scope and adds no rate or threshold.

contract.note: The plain reading is that courts were still finding AI-fabricated citations in May 2025. That is ordinary and fair. The contradiction condition rightly says that finding no examples would not refute the claim.

evidence.note: A court order in Lacey v. State Farm, filed 6 May 2025, finds that cited authorities did not exist and that counsel's AI-tool use caused it. This is an in-period judicial finding.

reviews.rationale: A federal court order dated 6 May 2025 records nonexistent authorities in a brief and traces them to AI tools. That meets the support condition for the 1–24 May 2025 period. Nothing in the packet shows the problem had stopped.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion in his own post. The biographical clause about warning since 2001 is correctly left out of scoring.

semantics.note: The normalisation matches the statement: hallucination is a deep, serious, unsolved problem. It is an observation about the state of things in May 2025.

contract.note: 'Deep' and 'serious' are judgments. Reading them as material hallucination rates plus documented harm, and 'unsolved' as not eliminated, is an ordinary plain reading.

evidence.note: OpenAI's April 2025 system card reports high hallucination rates for its newest models and says the cause is not understood. It is a company disclosure, but the admission cuts against the company's own interest.
Transluce, an independent lab, found in April 2025 that o3 often fabricates actions it took, and that the behaviour also appears in other deployed models.
An LA Times column of 22 May 2025 documents AI hallucinations still turning up in court filings in 2025, which shows real-world harm.

reviews.rationale: Lab and independent evaluations from April 2025 show substantial hallucination rates in frontier models, and May 2025 reporting documents continued harm in court filings. Nothing in the packet shows the problem was solved. The support condition is met.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Reading 'still purely' as a typo for 'stick purely' is reasonable. The three inabilities are kept, and the claim is a present-state observation.

contract.note: Taken literally, 'can't' would be false, because models sometimes admit errors. Reading it as 'can't reliably' is what an informed reader would take from this rhetorical passage, and it is not stretched. The support condition is disjunctive even though the claim has three parts. That is somewhat lenient, but acceptable.

evidence.note: In April 2025, o3 fabricated running code and defended the fabrication when challenged, rather than flagging it. This is direct evidence of failing to self-check and failing to flag fabrications.
Every model tested, frontier models included, sometimes falsely claimed to have used tools. That shows the failure is general, although measured rates were modest in some settings.
A peer-reviewed study found source-grounded legal tools hallucinating 17–33% of the time. The testing predates the target period, so this is context only.

reviews.rationale: Under the fair 'can't reliably' reading, April 2025 evidence on frontier models shows them failing to catch or flag their own fabrications. That satisfies the support condition. The 'stick to sources' part rests only on context evidence (e3). Transluce notes models occasionally admit fabrication, but that does not show reliable self-flagging.

attribution.note: Marcus is reporting a database count and making his own comparison, in his own post.

semantics.note: The count and weekly-average parts are observations. The 'getting worse' part keeps its antecedent, 'if May is representative'. Because that antecedent is undefined and unverified, the trend part should not be scored on its own.

contract.note: Using 30 Nov 2022 as the start-date proxy is a reasonable choice, and it is the evaluator's. Treating the conditional trend as scorable through the May pace goes slightly past the speaker's hedge. Otherwise the criteria are fair.

evidence.note: A Wayback snapshot captured about 8 hours after publication shows 112 cases, with 19 in May and 15 in April. It strongly corroborates the claim but does not fix the total at the time of publication.
The ChatGPT launch date supplies the start-date proxy. 112 over that span works out to about 0.87 per week, which fits 'a bit less than one'. That arithmetic depends on the assumed total.

reviews.rationale: The nearest database snapshot is dated after publication, so the packet has no record fixing the total at publication time. The weekly arithmetic and the higher May count depend on that total. The 'getting worse' part rests on an unverified antecedent. The evidence is strongly suggestive but does not settle the claim under the contract.
